generativity.notes: B and D have the same deep structure, nearly participant for participant: Failure, diagnoser, ArgType table, finalize, a probe-generating walker and a non-record list. They differ in detail: B keeps records as dicts and plugs types in with add_type, while D uses OpRecord and ArgSpec objects whose spec holds the type object, takes types in the constructor, and makes its consumers fully type-agnostic. A shares the record discipline (strict keys, consistency checks, samples bound at registration) but merges binder and diagnoser and keeps types as strings. C and E are monolithic registries with type switches and tolerant records; E departs further by following redirects.

worse_is_better: A reaches the refusal quality of B and D, and exceeds it (the fix keeps the caller's values, all problems are reported, samples are bound at registration), with fewer participants. It has no Failure value class, no separate diagnoser, no lazy finalize state machine and no non-record list module. That extra machinery in B and D does not pay for itself in this task: the Failure/diagnoser split never has a second producer, and lazy finalize adds a failure mode (one bad plug-in breaks every bind). The one extra this task does need, visible in NEXT.md, is B and D's ArgType seam. A plus a small type object would be the simplest design that grows. C is simpler still, but it buys that by dropping honesty (ignored keys, prose fixes, raw exceptions).
chapter_lessons: The walker and side effects: all five walkers run every sample for real with confirmation granted (impl-A/hubreg/registry.py:248, impl-B/hubreg/walker.py:179, impl-C/hubreg/registry.py:719, impl-D/hubreg/walker.py:133, impl-E/hubreg/registry.py:624), so walking a live hub locks the door. The chapter should name the force that an effectful operation needs a simulated implementation or a fake device for the walk, and how confirm-flagged records are walked.

Define 'fix' as a replayable call in the binder's own input vocabulary. The five implementations produced five dialects: a full call with the caller's values (A), a call without the kind (B), prose (C), a mix of full call, fragment and ' (confirmed)' (D), and CLI commands (E).

Say in the Solution, not only in note 8, that redirects are offered and never followed, and that lookup is exact on (kind, name). One implementation follows option, action, case-insensitive and cross-kind matches (impl-E/hubreg/registry.py:168-170,273-298).
State the identity key for host policy. confirm_required by bare name against (kind, name) is a security trap: B ignores dotted names (impl-B/hubreg/registry.py:190).

Note 1 says cross-record checks run at the end of start-up but not what happens to the offending record. B and D made finalize lazy, so one plug-in's dangling redirect fails every bind, while A, C and E deferred to walk(). Say to refuse or quarantine that record and keep the rest serving.

Make the pluggable type own its validation keys, its wrong-value probe and its refusal code. B and D still check min, max and enum values outside the type, and their walkers keep type-name tables (impl-B/hubreg/walker.py:210, impl-D/hubreg/walker.py:324-334). Enum membership came out as E_ARG_TYPE in A and E and as E_ARG_RANGE in B, C and D, because the accept/check split decides the code.

The non-record list is ornament when no agent-callable name lives outside the registry. B's list is empty and its CLI list is already stale (impl-B/hubreg/manual.py:13-17), and D repeats the verbs three times. Say it is needed only for agent-reachable names, and that CLI verbs are not such names.

The cross-argument hook and fields-as-a-function went unnoticed by every implementation without the ArgType seam (A, C, E). The chapter should say that the hook is optional where no rule spans arguments, so its absence is a conscious choice rather than a gap.
